If P = NP: how long to break a pnp key

Say someone finds an algorithm that cracks any problem where a guess can be checked. How fast it runs is written nᵏ: the smaller k, the better the algorithm. Pick one below and see how long a top Nvidia rack (Vera Rubin NVL72) would take against each pnp key setting. Rough estimates.

Algorithm quality

The same, for every algorithm

Each grey line is one algorithm; the blue one is your pick. Dots are pnp's settings. Further right means a bigger job to check one guess. Hover for times.

What this means: common criminals, not the Galactic Federation

The one-time pad itself can't be broken by any of this: without its key, a pnp file stays unreadable at every setting on this page, however good the algorithm and however many racks. What these numbers are about is a stolen key file, locked with --protect, and the encrypted key drive (LUKS) it sits on.

  • Today (no fast P = NP algorithm): with a generated 7-word passphrase, breaking that lock is out of reach for anyone, states included. A weak passphrase you made up yourself can fall in days.
  • If P = NP: the lock is only as strong as the algorithm is bad. A thief with one rack is still kept out unless the algorithm is very good; a state with thousands of racks gets in once it's good enough. So --protect and an encrypted key drive stop common criminals, not a state with real resources.
  • What stops a state, even if P = NP: keeping the key physically out of reach, and splitting it into shares kept in different places (--shares). Any share set missing one share is pure noise to every algorithm.

Why the memory setting doesn't save the key

  • An attacker skips the passphrase. With the ciphertext as well as the locked key file, they search for the 256-bit ChaCha20 key directly and check each guess against a few known bytes of the file (a JPEG or PDF header). That check is tiny (about 6.5×10⁴ bit operations) and has no Argon2id or Balloon in it, whatever --kdf-memory was. So the top row above is the one that counts.
  • More memory only slows the passphrase route, the other rows. It matters against ordinary guessing (see the last row), not against a P = NP algorithm.
  • The pad itself is safe at every setting. Without --protect, or with a key file but no ciphertext, there's nothing to check a guess against: every plaintext of that length is equally possible. No algorithm helps, however good. The same goes for a share set missing one share.
  • A LUKS-encrypted key drive is about as hard as the ChaCha20 shortcut: checking an AES-256 key against one known sector is about the same size of job.
Table: every setting against every algorithm
Assumptions
  • Rack speed: Vera Rubin NVL72, 72 GPUs at about 1014 32-bit integer operations per second each: about 2×1017 bit operations per second per rack. Generous to the attacker. Cost: about $4 million per rack (hardware only; no power, cooling or building), so the slider's prices are a floor. World GDP is about $110 trillion a year.
  • Size of the check (n): ChaCha20 shortcut 6.5×104 (80 quarter-rounds as gates). Passphrase route: Argon2id at about 3.5×106 bit operations per 1 KiB block × 2 passes, plus Balloon-BLAKE2b at about 3×106 per 64-byte block over 2 rounds, each times log₂(blocks) for data-dependent memory access in a circuit.
  • Time = c·nk ÷ (rack speed × racks). The constant c defaults to 1, again generous.
  • Ordinary guessing (no P = NP): about 3×105 guesses per second per rack at 1 GiB, averaging half of the 7-word passphrase's 290.5 possibilities.
  • "A lifetime" means 80 years.
